problem: Foundation-model (LLM/COT) frontier selection in zero-shot object goal navigation relies on a single greedy reasoning pass, producing nonsensical or irrelevant frontier choices that make navigation unreliable (e.g., ESC uses a single LLM expert).
motivation: Reliable commonsense reasoning is vital for robots in dynamic real-world environments with unseen objects. Inspired by Portfolio Theory (diversification) and self-consistency (voting), the authors aggregate multiple diverse experts to lower the chance of irrational frontier choices.
key_idea: Use three diverse foundation-model experts (object-to-frontier, room-to-frontier, visual scene-layout) to each propose frontiers, then pick a frontier by unanimous or majority consensus with a closest-frontier fallback.
insight: Diversifying the reasoning perspective and voting improves over both a single expert and a single-expert majority-vote baseline (k=3/5 samples: HM3D SPL 18.9/19.1 vs 21.7 for consensus). The expert ablation shows the visual expert (SLE) helps most (SPL 19.6 alone vs 17.8/18.2 for O2F/R2F), and SLE combined with either text expert gives 21.7, since vision carries both room and object cues. Error analysis shows the gain comes from lower exploration error, while detection and planning errors are unchanged.
method: Mapping: builds a top-down semantic map from RGB-D and pose (following Chaplot et al.), with GLIP zero-shot detection of objects and room types (as in ESC); candidate frontiers are boundaries between free and unexplored space (as in PONI).
Object2Frontier expert (O2F): ChatGPT-3.5 selects frontiers based on the objects observed near each frontier.
Room2Frontier expert (R2F): ChatGPT-3.5 selects frontiers based on room types, e.g. study room for a desk.
Scene Layout Expert (SLE): GPT-4V takes RGB observations plus detected objects and rooms and reasons about the scene layout to choose frontiers.

Consensus Decision Making (CDM): takes the intersection of all three experts' picks; if empty, takes pairwise-majority frontiers; if still empty, falls back to the closest frontier; the final choice is ranked by distance to the robot.
Local navigation policy: Fast Marching Method path planning to the selected frontier or the detected target, producing discrete actions.

setting.backbone: ChatGPT-3.5 (O2F, R2F) + GPT-4V (SLE) + GLIP detector, all frozen
setting.action_space: discrete: move forward / turn left / turn right / stop (high-level frontier goals planned with FMM)

numbers_note: Tables are complete. The expert ablation (Table 3) reports only SPL (RoboTHOR analysis). The text on RoboTHOR repeats the HM3D sentences (SR 35.4 to 37.4, SPL 17.8 to 21.7), which do not match the RoboTHOR table values (34.5 to 36.8, 18.2 to 22.3).
results: The full method reaches SR/SPL 37.4/21.7 on HM3D and 36.8/22.3 on RoboTHOR, beating ESC (35.4/17.8 and 34.5/18.2) and CoW (RoboTHOR 26.7/16.9). It also beats the single-expert majority-vote baselines (k=5: 36.6/19.1 HM3D, 35.6/20.8 RoboTHOR). It produces more direct paths and fewer actions than ESC.
limitations: System complexity and computational cost (multiple LLM/MLLM calls per step) hinder real-time use.
Nonsensical reasoning still occurs occasionally, and consensus can fail, requiring a closest-frontier fallback.
Detection error remains unchanged (~40%) since the same detector is used, and there is no real-robot evaluation despite the real-world claims.
